content.thinking:
I'm planning the full scene layout in one pass: a sandy island disc with a central pond, palm trees with curved trunks and swept fronds, striped tents, and simplified camel shapes built from capsules, all designed to avoid needing joint rigging.

Since the SDK requires exactly one root joint, I'll set a single root ("base") plus maybe a hinge joint for a tent flap, keeping the rig minimal and low-risk. I'm keeping scale toy-like, with a 2.4m diameter base, miniature camels around 0.35m tall, and the tallest palm near 1.3m, sticking to safe primitives like lathe, sweep, extrude, and rod with flat shading for a low-poly look, and starting the base outline from the axis outward.

Writing the lathe profile and sand dune details...

For the oasis I'm placing a shallow cylindrical water disc with teal mottled paint, surrounded by a ring of small dodecahedron stones generated in a loop, keeping part counts modest. I'm defining a helper function that wraps part creation with shared bone and placement defaults to cut down repetition.

Now I'm building a palm tree generator — curved trunk sweeps with grain-striped bark, a crown of coconut spheres, and fronds made from extruded leaf outlines drooping outward from the top.

Defining frond segment outlines...

Still working out tree geometry...

I'm scaling the camel to real proportions first—roughly 2m body length in camel-meters, then applying a 0.2 scale factor to get the toy size. I'm laying out body, hump, neck, and head as ellipsoids positioned along those real-world-ish coordinates before shrinking everything down.

Now I'm detailing the head features—muzzle, eyes, ears—and building out the four legs as curved sweeps with knee bends, plus hooves, a tufted tail, and a striped saddle blanket draped over the back.

Actually simpler: I'll make a girth-strap band by slightly enlarging an ellipsoid section around the body's belly at the narrower z-point where the body naturally tapers, giving a blanket-like ring that pokes outward just enough to read as a draped covering, colored red.

For colors, I'm going with a sandy tan base, a darker brown for shading, and a lighter cream for the muzzle, plus some mottling and countershading across the body for a painterly look. I'm making the design whimsical and chubby—shorter legs, a bigger head, and exaggerated roundness—while building a helper function that constructs each ellipsoid part from a low-poly sphere scaled and transformed into place via the body's coordinate system.

I'm planning a transform helper that scales and positions points with ground offsets, then setting up two standing camels plus one resting camel with folded legs for variety, lowering its body and bending its legs into horizontal folds to convey a reclining pose.

Setting leg contact point near ground level, then working out body center height so legs and torso sit correctly on the sand, with a dy offset applied to shift the hump, neck, and head together. For the tents, I'm planning a pyramidal Bedouin-style tent using a low-segment cone geometry rotated into a four-sided pyramid shape with striped texturing.

For the stripes, I'm computing the angle around the tent's vertical axis and alternating colors based on angular slices, giving a painted vertical-panel effect. I'm using a lathe with octagonal segments for a low-poly cone roof, topped with a gold finial sphere and a dark arched doorway cutout.

For tent B, I'm sketching a Bedouin-style flat canopy as a tilted box with four pole supports, blue/cream stripe coloring along the x-axis, and a scalloped valance made of small triangle shapes along the edge. For the doorway on tent A, I'm adding hinged flap triangles extruded from the arch opening to look like fabric panels that could fold open.

Actually, I'll skip the pose rotation and just build the flap geometry already pulled open, tied aside with ropes, so the joint is just for reference rather than driving rotation. Now I'm working out the tent's door geometry in local coordinates—placing the cone base, height, and an arched door extrusion relative to each tent's position and facing direction.

For the door itself, I realize trying to align an octagonal face normal to the door direction is fiddly since the lathe's spin angle is unclear, so instead I'll just float a dark triangular panel slightly in front of the cone surface as a simpler stand-in for the door opening, since a flat plane can't follow the cone's slope anyway.

I realize I can control the cone's face orientation with thetaStart, setting it to π/8 so a flat face centers at +Z with vertices at ±22.5°. That face sits at distance 0.9239R at the base, shrinking linearly with height, so I can position the door plate precisely on that sloped face by computing the distance at the chosen base height.

Working out the door outline shape in local slope coordinates, with an offset for thickness and direction vectors for extrusion along the slope... calculating face width at height since the octagonal face narrows as it rises.

Checking door and arch widths against the octagon face scale, the overlap seems minor enough to ignore. I'll simplify by narrowing the outline shape itself, tapering from a base width down to a point for the tent silhouette, and move on to finalize the coordinates.

Adding small flap triangles beside the door for visual detail, parented to the base joint with their own hinge bones, positioned at the door edges and tilted slightly outward along the tent's slope with a tiny offset so they sit just above the face surface.

I work out the outward normal vector for the tent's sloped surface using the rise and inward-offset components, then use it to push the door plate and flaps slightly off the roof face so they don't z-fight. For the roof stripes, I'm writing a paint function that computes an angle around the tent's vertical axis and alternates red and cream bands based on which angular segment a point falls in, though I need to be careful that the angle calculation accounts for the tent's yaw if it's rotated in world space.

Now I'm working out the stripe-face alignment math, then adding structural details: a trim ring at the cone base, a finial pole with a gold sphere topper, and a small pennant triangle.

For the guy-ropes, I'm computing anchor points along specific tent vertices and connecting them to ground pegs placed outward from the cone, using angle and radius math to position each rope realistically. Then I'll start on the second tent, an open-shade structure.

For the shade canopy, I'm placing four poles of differing heights to create a sloped roof, then computing the tilt angle from the height difference and figuring out the rotation needed so the canopy box aligns with that slope.

Working out quaternion composition for yaw and tilt...

For the canopy stripes, I'm figuring out a generic paint function that determines stripe coloring by projecting each point onto a local axis vector and flooring the result to pick between two colors.

Now I'm adding fringe details to the tent cloth—small downward-pointing cones along the front edge, alternating colors—and planning a textured rug for inside the tent using a diamond-patterned SVG placed flat on the ground.

I'm also laying out the oasis scene: several palm trees of varying heights, a camel scaled proportionally, a small pond offset from center with elliptical shape, and tents positioned toward the back facing the pond.

I'm adjusting palm, rock, and prop placements around the pond so nothing overlaps the water ellipse, nudging coordinates outward and adding rim stones, campfire glow, lantern, and crates for extra detail.

Tent B keeps pushing outside the base circle, so I need to shrink its canopy and reposition it closer to center, or just enlarge the overall base radius to around 1.35 so everything fits comfortably within the boundary.

Now I'm positioning the camels, calculating their facing angles so each one orients toward the pond based on the azimuth between their location and the pond center. I'm checking that their body lengths and head extensions stay within the overall scene radius without overlapping other elements.

I'm placing the campfire between the two tents, verifying it doesn't collide with the tents' edges, then adding logs, stones, and glowing orange flame cones around it. I'm also positioning the cactus, scattered rocks, and sacks near tent A, checking each against the pond's elliptical boundary to avoid overlap.

Now I'm setting up imports for the build file—math utilities, path helpers, texture painting functions, and a glow kit—making sure to only import what's actually used to avoid unused-import errors, then defining the base types and metadata before writing the main geometry code.

Writing quaternion helper function...

Then I define an ellipsoid helper for sphere-based parts with scaled radii, and I'm placing half-sunk ellipsoid dunes around the perimeter edges, checking whether they might project beyond the base boundary.

Now I'm building the lathe profile for the base shape with creased corners, then layering paints by height to create earth strata at the bottom and mottled sand texture up top, with another nested paint function distinguishing the rim coloring by normal direction.

For the pond, I'm planning a flattened cylinder scaled into an ellipse, positioned just above the sand surface, painted with a teal-to-cyan mottle to suggest shimmering water.

Still placing stones and reeds...

I'm confirming the spike sweep function supports bone attachment and reduced polygon sides for the cattail stalks, then moving into writing a palm tree generator function that builds a curved trunk path with fronds.

Writing trunk sweep code...

Defining zigzag frond outline points...

Writing scale helper function...

Now I'm figuring out the extrusion options for the frond geometry, computing direction vectors from azimuth/elevation angles and their perpendiculars to define segment orientation, then chaining segments end-to-end based on each segment's length.

I'm tallying up part counts per palm (trunk, bulb, coconuts, fronds with their midrib rods) to estimate total scene complexity across the four palms. Now I'm starting to define a camel-building function with parameters for position, yaw, scale, resting state, coat color, blanket color, and other traits.

Still writing camel transform logic...

Adding the hump shape and a blanket band around the body, with trim ellipsoids sized to stay just outside the body's radius at those z-offsets so they read as a decorative stripe.

Positioning the hanging tassel cones below the band, then sketching the neck as a swept tube with tapering radii along three control points to shape the camel's coat profile.

For the head I'm placing a tilted ellipsoid angled slightly downward, adding a smaller cream muzzle ellipsoid in front, and marking two tiny dark nostril spots near the muzzle tip.

I'm also adding a cream lower jaw ellipsoid tilted to match the muzzle, skipping a mouth line for simplicity, and setting up big whimsical white eye spheres angled outward on each side with room for dark pupils.

I'm checking that the eye placement stays inside the head's ellipsoid boundary so it peeks out naturally, adding small sparkle highlights, and sketching darker brow ridges above each eye. Now I'm starting to plan out the ears.

Adding a tuft cluster on top of the head, then working out leg geometry: standing poses with jointed path points and tapering radii for front and hind legs per side, making sure the leg tops tuck into the body and the bottoms taper into rounded hoof caps touching the ground.

Now I'm defining flat cylinder hooves with sole pads sized to the camel's scale so the feet sit flush on the ground, and sketching the hind leg's bent gait path with catmull interpolation between joints. I'm also working through folded leg positions for the resting pose, adjusting for the lowered body height.

Continuing, I'm placing the resting-pose leg paths with tapered radii so the hooves still touch ground zero, keeping the neck upright while resting, and sweeping a tail curve with a tapered radius ending in a dark tuft ellipsoid, adjusted for the resting body offset. Next I'm starting on a rein/halter piece running from the muzzle.

Calculating collar band tilt...

Checking the normalized direction confirms the ring orientation at the midpoint, with radius scaling to about .24 there. For the bell placement, I'm computing a perpendicular vector facing forward and downward from the neck axis, then positioning the gold sphere at roughly (0, 1.77, 1.26) using that offset.

Now I'm estimating total part counts—around 50 per camel, 150 for all three—and shifting to the tent geometry, reusing the same local-frame transform helper (T, Dv) I built for the camels to place tent structures with position, yaw, and scale parameters.

Writing frame transform code...

I'm building a cone-shaped tent with a painted canvas texture that creates alternating red/cream vertical stripes based on angular position around the cone, computing the angle offset to align the pattern with the tent's yaw rotation.

Now I'm working through the cone's vertex orientation to confirm the stripe pattern aligns correctly with the base, then adding a cylindrical valance skirt ring at the tent's base with alternating trim coloring.

I'm picking a cheerful palette - red, cream, teal, gold, brown - for the two tents and camel blankets, plus a small gold octagonal cap finial on top. Then I'm computing the slope normal vectors for positioning the door against the tent's angled surface.

Placing the door at the correct height and offset along that slope, extruding it in dark brown with a thin outward thickness, then adding a slightly larger gold arch trim just behind it to frame the doorway.

Now I'm adding the side flaps as triangular shapes next to the door, each attached via a hinge joint so they can swing open relative to the base.

Adding the pole with a gold ball tip and a small red pennant flag, then setting up rope and peg placements around the base at evenly spaced angles.

I'm picking which angular positions to use for the pegs, avoiding the one near the door at -π/8, and settling on a spread of index values around the circle instead.

For the cloth textures, I'm designing a helper function that paints each panel with a base color depending on its type, then blends in subtle noise to simulate a woven fabric look rather than flat solid color.

Now I'm moving to the second tent, a shade canopy structure, planning its four corner poles with specified heights and positions, plus the tilted canopy roof panel sitting above them.

Working out the slope angle for the canopy using arctan of the height difference over the span, then placing stripe patterns along the canopy's local x-axis by projecting points onto the axis and bucketing them. I'm also figuring out fringe decorations along the front edge of the canopy, accounting for the sloped height as a function of position.

For the fringe I'm placing small flipped cones in alternating colors across the front edge, plus a hanging back panel of cloth, and inside the tent I'm keeping a rug, two cushions, a teapot with tray, and a glowing lantern hung from the front support pole.

Writing rug SVG pattern...

I'm figuring out the quaternion rotation to orient the rug texture correctly without flattening normals, then sketching simple shapes for cushions and starting a lathe profile for the teapot body.

For the teapot I'm adding the tray, knob, spout, and handle as separate primitives, then designing the campfire scene with angled log rods, a ring of stone dodecahedra, cone-shaped flames, and an ember disc on the ground.

For the flames I'm layering an outer orange glow cone with a smaller yellow one inside, plus whimsical rising smoke puffs using shrinking pale spheres at increasing heights. For the cactus I'm sweeping a capsule-based trunk and arms with a greenish color, considering adding a pink flower on top and small spine dots for detail.

Now I'm adding scattered dodecahedron rocks in warm greys, plus camp props near the tents: tan sacks, wooden crates with grain textures and lid slats, and terracotta water jars built from a lathe profile.

Checking dune placements around the base so they don't overlap with the camel or base edge—several candidate positions conflict with existing elements, so I need to find spots that fit within the radius without clashing.

I'll place the camel's tail toward the back near (0.9,0.75) and add a smooth faceted dune at (0.35,1.05). For extra realism, I'm adding small scattered details—pebbles, grass tufts near the pond, and a trail of dark-sand footprint ellipses leading from the camel toward the pond to suggest a story of movement.

Now I'm checking placements so trunk bases and rim stones don't overlap the pond, then setting up layered cylinders for the water—darker inner layer for depth—and sizing lily pads to sit just above the water's surface.

I'm adding small pink flower cones to the lily pads, plus a couple of pale glinting ellipsoids to suggest light reflecting off the water. Skipping birds, extra decorations, and hanging signs to keep things simple, and I'm watching the overall color count to stay under the limit, remembering that mottled paint variations shouldn't count against it.

I'm checking the triangle budget — the spheres come out to roughly 80 triangles each, well within range — and working out total height: the tallest palm reaches about 1.21 units plus fronds brings it near 1.35, which fits the scene's proportions.

Now I'm writing the helper function that places a part on the base bone with flat shading, making sure the Fill type is correctly imported from the context module.

Writing the ellipsoid helper and sweep/tube helper functions...

Writing frond geometry function...

Still working out frond geometry...

I'm scaling palm fronds relative to trunk height, adding a few shorter, lighter young fronds near the crown's center, then moving on to building the tent's back wall.

Now I'm checking all the imports and helper functions I'm actually using so nothing gets left unused in the final file, and sketching a small rock-generation function using dodecahedron geometry squashed into an irregular boulder shape, positioned so its base sits on the ground.

I'm also designing crate props with wood boxes, corner slats, and a darker strap band for detail, plus sack shapes with ties, before composing the full scene and writing the final code carefully.

Working through tent peg placement using the ground-frame helper, and setting up camel geometry with scale-aware radii, tassels, resting poses, and coat coloring parameters like fur countershading and mottling for variety. Writing camel parameters...

Also adding darker fur at the hump cap, mane tufts along the neck, and pink cheek blush ellipsoids positioned against the head surface for a touch of character.
